copy.normal: Your CNS load is running {cns.acwr|1dp}× your four-week average — the point where extra work costs more than it returns. Take a deload week: same exercises, about a third fewer sets, and stop every set 2–3 reps short of failure.
copy.honest: {cns.acwr|1dp}× your four-week average and no deload in sight. You are not being hard, you are being slow. Take the week: same lifts, a third fewer sets, nothing near failure.

copy.normal: Your CNS is running high today — readiness {cns.readiness|pct}%. A good day for isolations and machines: keep the heavy compounds for your next session.
copy.honest: {cns.readiness|pct}% readiness. Whatever heroic compound you had planned today, it is going to be a bad rep at a weight you already own. Do isolations.

copy.normal: You are fully recovered — readiness {cns.readiness|pct}%. Work up to one heavy top set of 3–5 on your first compound, then back off about 10% for the rest.
copy.honest: {cns.readiness|pct}% readiness. No excuses available today. Work up to a heavy triple on your first lift and go and be heavy.

copy.normal: Your sleep tracks closely with how hard your sets feel. After a short night, expect the same weights to feel heavier — drop the load 5–10% or take a set off rather than pushing through.
copy.honest: Your RPE follows your sleep almost one to one. After a bad night the same weights feel heavy, and that is not weakness. Cut 5–10% off the bar instead of running into the wall to prove a point.

copy.normal: {volume.weeklySets:Chest|int} chest sets against {volume.weeklySets:Rear Delts|int} rear delt sets this week. If your shoulders complain on bench, that ratio is why — add 3 sets of face pulls or reverse pec-deck flyes to your next pull day.
copy.honest: {volume.weeklySets:Chest|int} sets of chest and {volume.weeklySets:Rear Delts|int} of rear delts. Then you wonder why your shoulders hurt on bench. That is not bad luck, that is arithmetic. Three sets of face pulls on your next pull day.

copy.normal: {volume.pushPct|int}% of your sets this week went to pushing. Pulling builds the shoulders that let you keep pushing — add 2 sets of rows or pull-downs to each session until the split evens out.
copy.honest: {volume.pushPct|int}% push. You are building the half of your body you can see in the mirror and quietly skipping the half that holds it together. Two extra sets of rows every session.

copy.normal: {volume.weeklySets:Quads|int} quad sets against {volume.weeklySets:Chest|int} for chest this week. Legs carry everything else — give them a real session, starting with 4 hard sets of squats or leg press.
copy.honest: {volume.weeklySets:Quads|int} sets of quads. Your upper body is thriving and your legs have been quietly retired. Hercul is not angry, just disappointed. Four sets of squats or leg press, this week.

copy.normal: {volume.weeklySets:Quads|int} quad sets this week but only {volume.weeklySets:Hamstrings|int} for hamstrings. That imbalance loads the knees — add 3 sets of Romanian deadlifts or seated leg curls before the week is out.
copy.honest: {volume.weeklySets:Quads|int} sets of quads, {volume.weeklySets:Hamstrings|int} of hamstrings. The back of your legs is not decoration. Three sets of Romanian deadlifts or leg curls before Sunday.

copy.normal: {volume.weeklySets:Chest|int} chest sets this week — past the point most people can recover from. Cap chest at roughly 16–20 hard sets and move the rest into back or legs.
copy.honest: {volume.weeklySets:Chest|int} chest sets. You are not training chest any more, you are just visiting it repeatedly. Stop at 20 and put the rest into your back.

copy.normal: You are averaging {nutrition.proteinAvg7dG|int} g of protein a day against your {nutrition.proteinTargetG|int} g target — {nutrition.proteinGap7dG|int} g short. A 200 g pot of Greek yogurt (about 20 g) plus a scoop of whey (about 25 g) closes most of that.
copy.honest: {nutrition.proteinAvg7dG|int} g of protein against a {nutrition.proteinTargetG|int} g target. You are paying for the gym and refusing to collect. Find {nutrition.proteinGap7dG|int} g: a shake and a yogurt does it.

copy.normal: You are averaging {nutrition.kcalAvg7d|int} kcal a day against a {nutrition.kcalTarget|int} kcal target — {nutrition.kcalOver7d|int} kcal over while cutting. Either eat to the plan or move the target on purpose. Oils, dressings and snacks are where that gap usually hides.
copy.honest: {nutrition.kcalAvg7d|int} kcal a day on a {nutrition.kcalTarget|int} kcal target. That is not a cut, that is maintenance with extra paperwork. Find the {nutrition.kcalOver7d|int} kcal.

copy.normal: You are averaging {nutrition.kcalAvg7d|int} kcal a day against a {nutrition.kcalTarget|int} kcal target — {nutrition.kcalShortfall7d|int} kcal short while trying to gain. A banana with 30 g of peanut butter is about 300 kcal: add one before bed until the gap closes.
copy.honest: {nutrition.kcalAvg7d|int} kcal a day on a {nutrition.kcalTarget|int} kcal target. You cannot build a house and skip the bricks. You are {nutrition.kcalShortfall7d|int} kcal short — eat the banana and peanut butter.

copy.normal: Only {nutrition.daysLogged7d|int} of the last 7 days are logged, which is too little to draw conclusions from. Log tonight's dinner and tomorrow's breakfast and these notes get specific to you.
copy.honest: {nutrition.daysLogged7d|int} days logged this week. Hard to fix a diet nobody is willing to look at. Log tonight's dinner and tomorrow's breakfast.

copy.normal: Fibre is averaging {nutrition.fiberAvg7dG|int} g a day; aim for 25–35 g. Swapping white bread or rice for wholegrain and adding a portion of beans, lentils or berries gets you most of the way.
copy.honest: {nutrition.fiberAvg7dG|int} g of fibre a day. Your gut would like a word. Wholegrain instead of white, plus a portion of beans or berries daily.

copy.normal: {nutrition.proteinAvg7dG|int} g of protein a day against a {nutrition.proteinTargetG|int} g target, with {nutrition.daysLogged7d|int} days logged. This is the boring part that actually works. Keep it.
copy.honest: {nutrition.proteinAvg7dG|int} g protein and {nutrition.daysLogged7d|int} days logged. Fine. Hercul has nothing to complain about. Do not let it go to your head.

copy.normal: You are up {body.weightDeltaKg:14|abs} kg over two weeks while logging a deficit. Unless you have just started creatine, which holds water, some calories are going unlogged — oils and snacks are the usual suspects.
copy.honest: +{body.weightDeltaKg:14|abs} kg on the scale and a deficit in the app. Unless you are drinking creatine by the spoonful, you are eating food you are not logging. The math does not lie.

copy.normal: You are logging a surplus while the scale dropped {body.weightDeltaKg:14|abs} kg. Your real expenditure is running higher than the estimate — add food if you want to grow.
copy.honest: You log a bulk, the scale says -{body.weightDeltaKg:14|abs} kg. Stop eating like a bird and eat an actual surplus.

copy.normal: You are in a surplus and your squat has not set a new best in 14 days. Those extra calories are not turning into muscle — check your training volume, or sleep more.
copy.honest: A surplus and a squat that has not moved in 14 days. You are not bulking, you are just eating. Add volume or add sleep, then earn the food.

copy.normal: Your weight has moved {body.weightDeltaKg:21|abs} kg in three weeks while you are cutting. Nothing is broken — the intake just is not where you think it is. Weigh your portions for a week, or take another 200 kcal off.
copy.honest: Three weeks of cutting and {body.weightDeltaKg:21|abs} kg to show for it. Something is not making it into the log. Weigh your food for a week. Hercul is not angry, just disappointed.

copy.normal: Your bodyweight is flat over three weeks on a gaining phase. Add 200 kcal a day and hold it for a fortnight before judging it.
copy.honest: Three weeks of "bulking" and no bulk. You are eating like someone who is scared of the scale. Add 200 kcal a day.

copy.normal: {body.weightDeltaKg:14|abs} kg down in two weeks is faster than muscle survives. Ease the deficit by 150–250 kcal a day unless there is a reason for the hurry.
copy.honest: {body.weightDeltaKg:14|abs} kg gone in a fortnight. Some of that was muscle you spent a year earning. Add 200 kcal back and slow down.

copy.normal: Down {body.weightDeltaKg:14|abs} kg in two weeks — right in the range where weight comes off and muscle stays. Keep the plan exactly as it is.
copy.honest: {body.weightDeltaKg:14|abs} kg down in a fortnight, at a pace that keeps your muscle. Nothing to fix. Do not change a thing.

copy.normal: Up {body.weightDeltaKg:14|abs} kg in two weeks — a pace that is mostly muscle for most lifters. Hold your calories where they are.
copy.honest: +{body.weightDeltaKg:14|abs} kg in a fortnight is the speed a real bulk moves at. Leave the calories alone.

copy.normal: It has been {exercise.lastPerformedDays:barbell-back-squat|int} days since your last squat, while everything else is on schedule. Put it back at the front of your next lower session and start about 10% lighter than last time.
copy.honest: {exercise.lastPerformedDays:barbell-back-squat|int} days since you squatted. Everything else is going great. Funny, that. Start 10% lighter and squat first.

copy.normal: {session.daysSinceLastWorkout|int} days since your last session. Do not try to make it up — just do a normal workout today, and keep the first one about 10% lighter.
copy.honest: {session.daysSinceLastWorkout|int} days. The plan does not care why. Go and do a session, an ordinary one, today.

copy.normal: You have trained {session.sessionsThisWeek|int}× this week against your usual {session.sessionsPerWeek4w|1dp}. One workout before Sunday keeps the month on track.
copy.honest: {session.sessionsThisWeek|int} sessions this week, and you normally do {session.sessionsPerWeek4w|1dp}. The weekend is still there. Use it.

copy.normal: Your bench has not beaten its previous best in two weeks, across {exercise.performedLast30d:barbell-bench-press|int} sessions this month. Change the stimulus for two weeks: switch rep range (5×5 to 3×8, or the reverse) or add a paused-rep variation.
copy.honest: {exercise.performedLast30d:barbell-bench-press|int} bench sessions this month and no new best. Doing the same thing harder is not a plan. Switch the rep range for two weeks.

copy.normal: Your squat estimated 1RM is up {exercise.e1rmDeltaKg14d:barbell-back-squat|1dp} kg in two weeks. Keep the same progression and add the smallest plate next session rather than jumping.
copy.honest: Squat up {exercise.e1rmDeltaKg14d:barbell-back-squat|1dp} kg in two weeks. Good. Now do not get greedy: the smallest plate, next session.

copy.normal: {session.sessionsPerWeek4w|1dp} sessions a week for a month straight. That consistency is worth more than any single programme.
copy.honest: {session.sessionsPerWeek4w|1dp} sessions a week for four weeks. Hercul has checked twice and can find nothing wrong. Unsettling.

copy.normal: Your strength is climbing through a deficit. That is fatigue management and programming done right — keep it exactly as it is.
copy.honest: Strength up while in a deficit. That is the hard version and you are pulling it off. Do not get clever and change something.

copy.normal: You squat regularly at {profile.heightCm|int} cm. Longer femurs force more forward lean to keep the bar over midfoot, so a low-bar position or a heeled shoe usually buys back the depth you are fighting for. Worth a three-week trial.
copy.honest: {profile.heightCm|int} cm grinding high-bar squats. Your femurs are never going to make that look like the video. Go low-bar or put your heels up — it is leverage, not character.

copy.normal: Your sumo deadlift sits at {exercise.e1rmRatio:sumo-deadlift:barbell-back-squat|1dp}× your back squat. At {profile.heightCm|int} cm that is largely anatomy — a wide stance asks a lot of long femurs. Conventional often suits your build better; run it for a block and compare.
copy.honest: Your sumo barely clears your squat at {exercise.e1rmRatio:sumo-deadlift:barbell-back-squat|1dp}×. Some of that is being {profile.heightCm|int} cm and pulling the stance that punishes it. Pick conventional, commit to a block, then argue.

copy.normal: You bench often at {profile.heightCm|int} cm on {volume.weeklySets:Rear Delts|int} rear delt sets a week. Long arms mean a longer bar path and more triceps off the chest, and the shoulder spends longer at end range — direct rear delt and rotator cuff work is part of the lift, not an extra.
copy.honest: {profile.heightCm|int} cm of leverage against you on bench and {volume.weeklySets:Rear Delts|int} rear delt sets defending the joint. Long arms make that press a shoulder-health problem before it is a chest problem. Fix the back of the shoulder.

copy.normal: You pull conventional at {profile.heightCm|int} cm — a shorter build usually keeps the bar close and the back angle friendly here. Try a heavier top set before assuming sumo is the answer.
copy.honest: {profile.heightCm|int} cm pulling conventional. That is the stance your build is actually good at. Stop reading about sumo and add weight.

copy.normal: You squat {exercise.e1rmRatioBelted:barbell-back-squat|1dp}× more with a belt than without. Your legs clearly have the strength; your trunk is what holds them back — add 2–3 sets of planks or ab-wheel rollouts after squats.
copy.honest: Your belted squat is {exercise.e1rmRatioBelted:barbell-back-squat|1dp}× your raw squat. The belt is doing your abs' job. Fix the core, or your back pays for it.

copy.normal: You have relatively long femurs. For your upcoming squats, a low-bar position or a raised heel is usually more comfortable for keeping an upright torso.
copy.honest: Long femurs and a squat coming up. If you are doing high-bar in flat shoes, you are fighting your own mechanics. Try low-bar or lifting shoes.

copy.normal: With a longer arm span, bench pressing requires a greater range of motion. Consider a slightly wider grip to reduce shoulder strain at the bottom.
copy.honest: Long arms mean you have to press the bar an extra mile. Widen your grip a bit or you are just putting unnecessary wear on your shoulders.
